name: AI for Sales and Customer Experience
objectives: Given 15 possible leads from public information and your network, score them on problem, money, decision and timing and choose your top 10, with a written reason for each
Given two leads from your list, write short, personal outreach messages that follow US email, call and text rules, each with a real detail about the lead, your address and an opt-out line
Before a sales conversation, create a one-page call guide with five open questions and answers to your three most common objections, with every answer true and practiced once in an AI role-play
Given at least ten real customer questions with names removed, create a 10-question FAQ with answers drafted from your own facts, with every answer checked
Given a real or made-up complaint, choose a fair fix and write a calm reply using thanks, sorry, the fix and when, with the fix decided by you, not AI
Given at least 20 pieces of customer feedback, use AI to find the main themes and choose one improvement, after checking AI's counts yourself

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Finding and qualifying leads
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a short list of leads and decide which are most likely to buy.
This lesson builds toward: Given 15 possible leads from public information and your network, you will score them on problem, money, decision and timing and choose your top 10, with a written reason for each.
A lead is a person or business that might buy from you. Qualifying means deciding which leads are worth your time. A simple test: Do they have the problem you solve? Can they pay? Can they decide? Do they need it soon?
AI can help you brainstorm where your leads are ("Where do small gyms in my city look for cleaning services?") and score a list you already have. Describe each lead in general words and ask AI to sort them by the four questions.
Use public business information, not private personal data. Do not buy contact lists or scrape personal details; they are often out of date and can break privacy and marketing rules.
Step by step:
- Write who your best past customers were.
- Ask AI where similar businesses or people can be found.
- List 15 to 20 possible leads from public sources and your own network.
- Score each on problem, money, decision and timing.
- Keep the top 10 with a one-line reason each.
Words to know:
- Lead: a person or business that might buy from you.
- Qualify: decide whether a lead is likely to buy and worth your time.
Try it now: List 15 possible leads, score them on problem, money, decision and timing with AI's help, and keep your top 10 with a reason for each.
You can now find leads and focus on the ones most likely to buy.

options: Someone with the problem, the money, the say and a need soon
Anyone whose email you can find
A friend who likes your posts
check.why: Qualified leads meet the four questions: problem, money, decision and timing.

check.q: A lead loves your idea but has no budget until next year. What do you do?
options: Put them at the top of your list
Score them lower on money and timing and follow up later
check.why: Scoring helps you focus on who can buy now.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing personal outreach, not spam
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short, personal first message that follows US email, call and text rules.
This lesson builds toward: Given two leads from your list, you will write short, personal outreach messages that follow US email, call and text rules, each with a real detail about the lead, your address and an opt-out line.
Good outreach is short and about them: what you noticed about their business, the problem you can help with, and one easy next step. Ask AI: "Write a 70-word first email to a small gym owner. Mention that their reviews talk about clean locker rooms being important. Offer a free 15-minute walkthrough. No hype." Then add one detail only you know.
For commercial email, the CAN-SPAM Act requires honest From and subject lines, your physical address and a clear way to opt out, and opt-outs must be honored within 10 business days.
Calls and texts have stricter rules. Marketing texts and robocalls usually need the person's consent first, and in 2024 the FCC ruled that AI-generated voices count as "artificial" voices under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. Do not use AI voice calls or mass texts without consent, and check fcc.gov or a lawyer before you start.
Step by step:
- Note one real detail about the lead from public information.
- Ask AI for a short message: their situation, your help, one next step.
- Add a personal detail and check every fact.
- For email, include your address and an opt-out line.
- Do not text or AI-call anyone without their consent.
Words to know:
- Outreach: contacting a possible customer first.
- CAN-SPAM Act: US law with rules for commercial email.
- TCPA: Telephone Consumer Protection Act: US law limiting marketing calls and texts without consent.
Official sources:
- FTC: CAN-SPAM Act Compliance Guide for Business
- FCC: AI-generated voices in robocalls ruling (2024)
Try it now: Write two personal outreach emails to leads from your list with AI's help. Add a real detail to each, and check they include your address and an opt-out line.
You can now write personal outreach that respects email, call and text rules.

check.q: What must a commercial email include under CAN-SPAM?
check.why: Commercial emails must give a way to opt out.

check.q: AI writes an outreach email that could be sent to anyone. What do you do?
options: Add something real you noticed about this lead
check.why: A real detail makes the message personal, not spam.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Preparing for a sales conversation
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a one-page call guide with questions and answers to common objections.
This lesson builds toward: Before a sales conversation, you will create a one-page call guide with five open questions and answers to your three most common objections, with every answer true and practiced once in an AI role-play.
A sales conversation is mostly listening. Prepare five good questions about the customer's situation, problem and goals, then explain how you help in their words.
Objections are reasons people give for not buying: "It costs too much." "I need to think about it." "We already have someone." Ask AI: "List the five most common objections for [service] and give a calm, honest answer to each." Edit them so they sound like you and are true.
Role-play with AI: "Pretend you are a busy gym owner who is not sure about hiring a cleaning service. Ask me hard questions." Practice until you can answer without reading.
Step by step:
- Write five open questions about the customer's situation and goals.
- Ask AI for common objections and honest answers.
- Edit the answers so they are true and sound like you.
- Role-play the conversation with AI.
- Put it all on one page.
Words to know:
- Objection: a reason a customer gives for not buying yet.
- Role-play: practicing a conversation by acting it out.
- Open question: a question that cannot be answered with just yes or no.
Try it now: Build your one-page call guide: five open questions and honest answers to your three most common objections. Role-play once with AI.
You can now prepare for and practice a sales conversation with AI.

options: One that cannot be answered with just yes or no
check.why: Open questions get the customer talking about their needs.

check.q: AI's answer to the objection "I need to think about it" sounds pushy. What do you do?
options: Edit it so it is honest and sounds like you
Read it word for word faster
check.why: You edit AI answers to be true and in your own voice.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building a customer FAQ
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create a 10-question FAQ from the questions customers really ask.
This lesson builds toward: Given at least ten real customer questions with names removed, you will create a 10-question FAQ with answers drafted from your own facts, with every answer checked.
Customers ask the same questions again and again. A frequently asked questions (FAQ) page or document saves you time and helps customers decide faster.
Collect real questions from emails, messages and calls for two weeks (remove names and contact details). Ask AI to group them and write clear, short answers using only facts you give it: prices, hours, area, policies.
Check every answer. Then use the FAQ on your website, in your saved replies, and as the facts for any chatbot. If you use a chatbot, tell customers it is automated and give an easy way to reach a person.
Step by step:
- Collect customer questions for two weeks, without names or contact details.
- Ask AI to group them and pick the top 10.
- Give AI your real facts and ask for short answers.
- Check each answer.
- Publish the FAQ and use it in replies.
Words to know:
- FAQ: frequently asked questions: a list of common questions with answers.
- Chatbot: an automated program that answers customer messages.
Try it now: Collect at least ten real customer questions (no names), use AI to group them and draft answers from your facts, check each, and save your FAQ.
You can now turn real customer questions into a checked FAQ.

check.q: Where should FAQ questions come from?
check.why: Real questions make an FAQ that actually helps.

check.q: AI's FAQ answer gives a delivery time you do not offer. What do you do?
options: Correct it from your real facts
check.why: FAQ answers must be based on your facts.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Answering complaints calmly
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft a calm, fair reply to a complaint, and decide how to fix it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real or made-up complaint, you will choose a fair fix and write a calm reply using thanks, sorry, the fix and when, with the fix decided by you, not AI.
A complaint handled well can win a customer for life. A simple pattern: thank them, say sorry for their experience, say what you will do, and say when. Do not argue in public; offer to continue privately.
When you are upset, AI helps you stay calm. Summarize the complaint in your own words (no names or order numbers) and ask: "Draft a calm, short reply that thanks them, apologizes, offers [fix], and invites them to message us privately."
You decide the fix. Do not let AI promise refunds or credits you have not agreed to, and do not use AI to write fake positive reviews to bury the bad one; the FTC bans fake reviews, including AI-written ones.
Step by step:
- Read the complaint and wait a few minutes before replying.
- Decide the fair fix yourself.
- Summarize the complaint for AI with no names or order numbers.
- Ask for a calm reply: thanks, sorry, the fix, when, move to private.
- Edit, check and send.
Words to know:
- Complaint: a customer telling you something went wrong.
- Fix: what you will do to make it right, like a redo or refund.
Official sources:
- FTC: Final rule banning fake reviews and testimonials (press release)
Try it now: Take a real or made-up complaint, decide the fair fix, and use AI to draft a calm reply using the four-part pattern. Save it as your complaint-reply template.
You can now answer complaints calmly and fairly with AI's help, and decide the fix yourself.

check.q: What are the four parts of a calm complaint reply?
check.why: This pattern keeps replies calm, fair and clear.

check.q: AI's draft reply offers a full refund you have not agreed to. What do you do?
options: Decide the fair fix yourself and change the draft
check.why: You decide the fix; AI only drafts the words.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Learning from customer feedback
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to find patterns in reviews and feedback, and choose one improvement.
This lesson builds toward: Given at least 20 pieces of customer feedback, you will use AI to find the main themes and choose one improvement, after checking AI's counts yourself.
Reviews, survey answers and messages tell you what to fix and what to keep. Reading them one by one, you miss patterns. AI is good at grouping.
Copy 20 to 50 reviews or comments (remove names) and ask: "Group this feedback into themes. For each theme, say how many comments mention it and give one example. List the top three things customers love and the top three problems."
Check the counts by skimming yourself, because AI can miscount. Then choose one problem to fix this month, fix it, and tell customers you listened.
Step by step:
- Collect 20 to 50 reviews or comments and remove names.
- Ask AI to group them into themes with counts and examples.
- Skim to check the themes and counts.
- Choose one problem to fix this month.
- Tell customers what you changed.
Words to know:
- Theme: a topic that comes up again and again in feedback.
- Survey: a short set of questions you ask customers.
Try it now: Final task: analyze at least 20 pieces of feedback with AI, choose one fix, then assemble your sales and service kit: 10 qualified leads, two outreach messages, call guide, FAQ and complaint template.
You can now use AI across sales and service: find leads, reach out properly, prepare, answer customers and keep improving.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Qualified leads Fewer than 10 leads, no reasons, or leads from unapproved sources. 10 leads from public information or your network, each with a reason. Each lead shows its score on problem, money, decision and timing. Outreach messages Generic, or missing the address or opt-out line. Two short, personal messages with a real detail, address and opt-out. Each ends with one easy next step and was read aloud before sending. Call guide Missing questions or objection answers, or answers overpromise. Five open questions and honest answers to three objections, practiced once. Notes what was changed after the role-play. FAQ and complaint template FAQ answers unchecked, or the complaint reply promises a fix not decided. 10 checked FAQ answers and a four-part complaint template with the owner's fix. The FAQ is published or in use, and the template has a line offering to continue privately. Private data Customer names or contact details went into an AI tool. All questions and feedback had names and contact details removed. Notes the AI tool's data setting that was checked. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a theme in customer feedback?
options: A topic that comes up again and again
check.why: Themes show the problems many customers share.

check.q: AI says most feedback is about price, but you remember many comments about wait times. What do you do?
options: Ask AI to agree with you
Skim the feedback yourself to check
check.why: Check AI's counts yourself before acting on them.
